title: Lose 90% of a forest, 90% of species?
hook: A forest is cut to a tenth of its size. Does it keep a tenth of its species?

doesNotKnow: the species-area rule S = cA^z with z about 0.25
that species fall much less steeply than area, but still fall

misconception: Losing 90% of the area loses 90% of the species.
objective: The learner can explain that with species proportional to area^0.25, keeping 10% of a forest eventually keeps about 56% of its species: far more than 10%, but still a loss of almost half.

claims.text: Species number tends to rise with habitat area as S = cA^z, with z typically about 0.15 to 0.35; 0.25 is a common textbook value.
claims.source: MacArthur R.H. & Wilson E.O. (1967) The Theory of Island Biogeography, Princeton; Rosenzweig M.L. (1995) Species Diversity in Space and Time, Cambridge, ch. 2.

claims.text: With z = 0.25, keeping 10% of the area keeps 0.1^0.25 = 56% of species, and keeping 50% keeps 84%.
A small piece of habitat still holds many species because many species are spread across much of the original area.
claims.source: Rosenzweig (1995) ch. 2 (sampling explanation of the species-area relation).

claims.text: The species-area rule is an empirical regularity, not a law, and losses after habitat is cut take years to decades to arrive (extinction debt).
claims.source: Tilman D., May R.M., Lehman C.L. & Nowak M.A. (1994) Habitat destruction and the extinction debt, Nature 371:65-66; Rosenzweig (1995).

claims.text: The forest of 100 patches and 100 species is made up; which species disappear follows an untuned shuffled order and only their number comes from the rule.

recall.question: With species proportional to area^0.25, a reserve keeps 1% of an old forest. Roughly what share of species does it eventually keep?
recall.why: 0.01^0.25 = 0.32. Species fall much less steeply than area, but losing 99% of the area still loses about two thirds of them.
